title: Bharata's journey
hook: a prince sets out with an army to give a crown away, and at every stop someone thinks he's come to kill
carry: bharata's love comes to give, not take

segments.voice: Yesterday: dharma before the crown. Bharata swore his innocence to Kausalya and gave his father the last rites.

The ministers gather and do the obvious thing: they offer Bharata the throne. He says no, in front of everyone. The eldest son is king. I'm going to the forest to bring Rama home, and if he won't come, I'll stay there in his place. Then he sets out, and not quietly. Road builders go ahead clearing a path. Behind him come the queens, the priest Vasishtha, the citizens and an army. Which, from a distance, looks exactly like what it isn't.
screen: `THE ELDEST SON IS KING.` → `ROAD BUILDERS GO AHEAD.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE AN INVASION.`

segments.voice: Watch the road, because the same scene happens three times. First, the Ganga at Shringaverapura. Guha, the boatman king who ferried Rama across, sees the army and tells his people to guard the river. Why would Bharata need soldiers, unless he means Rama harm? He meets Bharata with gifts and a careful question. Bharata answers plainly, and Guha believes him. Then Guha shows him the spot under the tree where Rama and Sita slept on a bed of grass, and tells how Lakshmana stood watch all night. Bharata sees the crushed grass and is overwhelmed. Second, Bharadvaja's hermitage, where Rama stayed too. The sage welcomes him, then asks outright: you're not here to harm an innocent man, are you? Bharata is hurt, and answers again. The sage believes him, and by the power of his austerity feeds the whole army a feast fit for the gods. Third, Chitrakoot. Lakshmana climbs a tall sal tree, sees the dust and the banners of Ayodhya, and wants to fight. Bharata has come to finish us, he says. Rama stops him. Bharata loves us more than his own life. He hasn't come for that. Three times, the same suspicion. Twice it takes a conversation to clear it. The third time, Rama doesn't need one. He already knows his brother. And Hindu tradition never forgot this brother. Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, gives Bharata's love for Rama some of his most moving pages, and many devotees hold Bharata up as a model of bhakti, devotion: love that comes to give, not to take. Everyone on that road saw an army. Rama saw a heart that wanted nothing for itself.
screen: `GUHA GUARDS THE RIVER.` · `THE GRASS BED UNDER THE TREE.` · `BHARADVAJA ASKS OUTRIGHT.` · `LAKSHMANA UP THE SAL TREE.` · `RAMA ALREADY KNOWS HIM.` · then, large: `BHAKTI: LOVE THAT COMES TO GIVE.`

segments.voice: Picture one person you trust without needing proof, the way Rama trusts Bharata, and notice what that trust is built on: years, small kept promises, how they treated you when it cost them something. Let a little gratitude rise, and stay with it.
Bharata's journey. Guha suspects him, Bharadvaja questions him, Lakshmana wants to fight him. Rama alone says: he comes in love.
Your line: Bharata's love comes to give, not take. Everyone saw an army; Rama saw his brother's heart. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often follow Bharata's road through the same stops Rama made, Guha's river and Bharadvaja's hermitage, so the two journeys mirror each other.

original.note: Sanskrit bharata: Rama's brother's name. a different, older King Bharata is the one tradition links to Bhārata, a name for India.

Shringaverapura.meaning: the town on the Ganga where Guha ruled

Guha.meaning: the boatman king who ferried Rama across the Ganga

Bharadvaja.meaning: the sage at Prayaga, where the rivers meet

Vasishtha.meaning: the royal priest and teacher of Rama's family

sal.meaning: a tall forest tree of India
